'''William Lax''' {{post-nominals|post-noms=[[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]]}} (1761 – 29 October 1836) was an English astronomer and mathematician who served as [[Lowndean Professor of Astronomy and Geometry]] at the [[University of Cambridge]] for 41 years.

Lax was born in [[Ravensworth]] in the [[North Riding of Yorkshire]]. He attended [[Trinity College, Cambridge|Trinity College]], Cambridge and graduated [[Bachelor of Arts]] as the [[Senior Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|Senior Wrangler]] and first [[Smith's Prize]]man of his year. He was elected a [[fellow]] of Trinity College, ordained as a minister, and received his [[Master of Arts (Oxbridge and Dublin)|Master of Arts]]. Lax was granted the [[Living (Christianity)|living]]s of vicar of [[Marsworth]], [[Buckinghamshire]] and of [[St Ippolyts]] near [[Hitchin]], [[Hertfordshire]], where he erected an [[observatory]].

Lax was best known for his ''Remarks on a Supposed Error in the Elements of Euclid'' (1807) and his work regarding the ''[[Nautical Almanac]]'', which was an important reference for navigation in the period. An obituary claimed that "To whatever Professor Lax applied, he made himself completely master of it". His daughter married [[Andrew Amos (lawyer)|Andrew Amos]] and through that line Lax is the grandfather of [[Sheldon Amos]] and the great grandfather of [[Maurice Amos]], a notable legal dynasty.

==Early life==
[[File:The Old Grammar School, Kirby Hill - geograph.org.uk - 1626080 (cropped).jpg|thumb|upright|left|The former grammar school at Kirby Hill]]
Lax was born in the village of [[Ravensworth]], near [[Richmond, North Yorkshire|Richmond]] in the [[North Riding of Yorkshire]], England, the son of William (1731 – 19 August 1812) also born in Ravensworth, and Hannah Lax (1738 – 10 June 1811).<ref name=autogenerated9>A. M. Clerke, 'Lax, William (1761–1836)’, rev. Anita McConnell, Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, Oxford University Press, 2004 [http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/16213, accessed 30 April 2012]</ref> He was christened on 27 October 1761 in [[Burneston]]. He was educated at the Kirby Ravensworth Free Grammar School, where he learned [[Latin]] (in which he became fluent) and [[Greek language|Greek]] as well as [[English language]], [[arithmetic]] and mathematics.<ref name=autogenerated9 /><ref>{{Cite newspaper The Times |title=In The Matter of the Kirby Ravensworth Free Grammar School |department=Vice-Chancellors' Courts, Saturday, 27 May |date=29 May 1843 |page=7 |issue=18308 |column=F }}</ref> Although the school was subsidised by a charitable trust, "Free" in the context of the school's name meant free from all authority save for the Crown.

Lax was admitted as a [[sizar]] to [[Trinity College, Cambridge|Trinity College]], [[Cambridge University]] on 22 November 1780 at the age of 19. Trinity was at the time the richest college at Cambridge.<ref name="Linehan2011">{{cite book|last=Linehan|first=Peter|title=St John's College Cambridge: A History|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UHir3e7Y_jUC&pg=PA120|access-date=26 July 2012|date=21 April 2011|publisher=Boydell Press|isbn=978-1-84383-608-7|page=209}}</ref> Sizars were students who were not of the [[gentleman]]ly class, who were charged lower fees and obtained free food and/or lodging and other assistance during their period of study in exchange for performing work at their colleges.<ref name=autogenerated13>{{cite book|last=Linehan|first=Peter|title=St John's College Cambridge: A History|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UHir3e7Y_jUC&pg=PA120|access-date=26 July 2012|date=21 April 2011|publisher=Boydell Press|isbn=978-1-84383-608-7|pages=120–121}}</ref> By the eighteenth century, sizars were fully integrated members of the community, who were as likely to be employed by Fellow commoners as companions rather than servants.<ref name=autogenerated13 /> They were expected to wait at table (as were [[Pensioner#Other uses|pensioners]] and scholars), but by the eighteenth century they had their own gyps (servants) and bedmakers.<ref name=autogenerated13 />

Lax [[Matriculation#United Kingdom|matriculated]] in the [[Michaelmas term]] of 1781 and became a private tutor to [[John Pond]], later [[Astronomer Royal]].<ref name=autogenerated10>{{cite journal |date=1837 |journal=The London and Edinburgh Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science |volume=LX |page=146 |title=The Royal Society. Address of His Royal Highness the President (pp. 141–154)|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-EwwAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA146}}</ref><ref name="Society1839">{{cite book|author=Royal Astronomical Society|title=Monthly notices of the Royal Astronomical Society|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=y7lAAAAAYAAJ&pg=RA1-PA185|access-date=2 July 2012|volume=4-6|date=1839|publisher=Priestley and Weale|page=33}}</ref> Lax was elected a scholar (i.e. one on a scholarship) of Trinity in 1784; [[John Cranke]] and Henry Therond were his [[tutor]]s, a role which would have seen them not only teaching Lax, but also acting in the role of ''[[in loco parentis]]''.<ref name=autogenerated2>Admissions to Trinity College, Cambridge Edited by W. W. Rouse Ball and J. A. Venn, [https://brittlebooks.library.illinois.edu/brittlebooks_open/Books2009-06/trinco0001admtri/trinco0001admtriv00003/trinco0001admtriv00003_ocr.txt accessed 8 May 2012]</ref> Lax was conferred a [[Bachelor of Arts]] (B.A.) in 1785 and graduated as the [[Senior Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|Senior Wrangler]] and was awarded the first [[Smith's Prize]] of his year.<ref name=autogenerated9 /> Until 1790, all examinations at Trinity were written in Latin.<ref name=autogenerated15>{{cite book|last=Linehan|first=Peter|title=St John's College Cambridge: A History|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UHir3e7Y_jUC&pg=PA120|access-date=26 July 2012|date=21 April 2011|publisher=Boydell Press|isbn=978-1-84383-608-7|page=208}}</ref>

==Career==

===Early career===
In 1785 Lax was appointed [[Curate#Anglican Communion|curate]] of [[Tideswell]] in the [[Peak District]] of [[Derbyshire]] with an annual [[stipend]] of £35.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://blog.theclergydatabase.org.uk/jsp/DisplayAppointment.jsp?CDBAppRedID=111849|title=Appointment record 111849, Linked to person: Lax, William 1785-1801|work=[[Clergy of the Church of England database]]|access-date=2025-12-16}}</ref> In 1786, as was essentially the due of Senior Wranglers, he was elected a [[fellow]] of Trinity College.<ref>A Cambridge Alumni Database, Cambridge University Library, [http://venn.lib.cam.ac.uk/cgi-bin/search.pl?sur=&suro=c&fir=&firo=c&cit=&cito=c&c=all&tex=LS780W&sye=&eye=&col=all&maxcount=50 accessed 8 May 2012] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121012020334/http://venn.lib.cam.ac.uk/cgi-bin/search.pl?sur=&suro=c&fir=&firo=c&cit=&cito=c&c=all&tex=LS780W&sye=&eye=&col=all&maxcount=50 |date=12 October 2012 }}</ref> According to [[Peter Linehan]], fellows at this time, "were becoming richer, living and behaving more like gentlemen".<ref name="Linehan2011" /> He was [[ordained]] as a [[Minister (Christianity)|minister]] in 1787 at [[Peterborough]] and received his [[Master of Arts (Oxbridge and Dublin)|Master of Arts]] (M.A.) in 1788.<ref>Country News..     The Times (London, England), Monday, 17 March 1788; p. 3.</ref> He was a moderator from 1789 to 1791 which entailed him presiding over oral examinations which were then necessary for the B.A. to be awarded. As a moderator Lax was responsible for the introduction of "very high flown compliments, and at the same time extending the disputations to double the usual length, which was around one hour and ten minutes" which "sent a ripple through tradition" according to [[Greg Dening]].<ref>{{cite book |title=Unreformed Cambridge: A Study of Certain Aspects of the University in the Eighteenth Century |last=Winstanley |first=Denys Arthur |date=2009 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=9781108002295 |page=350 }}</ref><ref name="Dening1995">{{cite book|author=Greg Dening|title=The Death of William Gooch|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=f07IuBDw6qYC|access-date=2 July 2012|date=1 October 1995|publisher=Melbourne University Publish|isbn=978-0-522-84692-8|page=106}}</ref> Dening argues that this was, "Lax's way of getting into the act and making Acts flourish".<ref name="Dening1995" /> In 1791 he was appointed as a [[taxor]] by the University.<ref>"News." St. James's Chronicle or the British Evening Post [London, England] 13 October 1791 – 15 Oct. 1791: n.p. 17th and 18th Century Burney Collection. Web. 21 January 2013.</ref> Lax was an assistant tutor from 1797 until 1801, but resigned when he married Margaret Cradock, as College fellows were not permitted to marry.<ref name=autogenerated2 /><ref name="Wright1827">{{cite book|author=John M. F. Wright|title=Alma Mater or Seven Years at the University of Cambridge: in Two Volumes|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0J9LAAAAcAAJ|access-date=2 July 2012|date=1827|publisher=Black, Young and Young|page=169}}</ref>

===Lowndean Chair===
[[File:WrenCambridge.JPG|thumb|upright|right|Wren Library, Trinity College, Cambridge.]]

In 1795 Lax was appointed [[Lowndean Professor of Astronomy and Geometry]] in succession to [[John Smith (astronomer)|John Smith]]. The position was a [[sinecure]] with an annual salary initially of around £300, later rising to around £500 per annum by 1821.<ref name=autogenerated7>{{cite news |title=To Mr. Brougham, and the gentlemen for the committee for investigating abuses in public charity schools, &c. |author=Thos. Lowndes. |newspaper=The Morning Post (London, England) |date=3 May 1821 }}</ref><ref name=autogenerated5>{{cite book|author=John M. F. Wright|title=Alma Mater or Seven Years at the University of Cambridge: in Two Volumes|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0J9LAAAAcAAJ|access-date=2 July 2012|date=1827|publisher=Black, Young and Young|page=170}}</ref> Cambridge had two astronomical chairs, and the Lowndean was seen as the more theoretical and less experimental of the two. During Lax's tenure a mathematical chair was seen as "a prize or a means of securing leisure, and at best, merely as offering a position where a man could pursue his own researches undisturbed by other duties".<ref name="Ball1908">{{cite journal|title=The Cambridge School of Mathematics|first=W. W.|last=Rouse Ball|author-link=W. W. Rouse Ball|journal=[[The Mathematical Gazette]]|volume=6|issue=99|date=July 1912|pages=311–323|doi=10.2307/3605019|jstor=3605019}} Quote is from p. 315.</ref> In 1816 Lax was described as holding the professorship with "great reputation".<ref name="WatkinsShoberl1816">{{cite book|author1=John Watkins|author2=Frederic Shoberl|title=A biographical dictionary of the living Authors of Great Britain and Ireland: comparising literary memoirs and anecdotes of their lives; and a chronological register of their publications, with the number of editions printed; including notices of some foreign writers whose works have been occasionally published in England|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-ndLAAAAcAAJ|access-date=2 July 2012|date=1816|publisher=Colburn|page=199}}</ref> The sole duty of Lax's professorship was that he was required to examine students annually for the Smith's Prize, including [[John Herschel]], [[Adam Sedgwick]], [[George Biddell Airy]] and [[William Cavendish, 7th Duke of Devonshire]].<ref name="AiryAiry2010">{{cite book|author1=George Biddell Airy|author2=Wilfred Airy|title=Autobiography of Sir George Biddell Airy|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=f1zaHfblHvUC|access-date=2 July 2012|date=24 June 2010|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-108-00894-5|page=40}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Passages from the Life of a Philosopher |last=Babbage |first=Charles |date=1864 |publisher=Longman |access-date=5 July 2012 |url=https://archive.org/stream/passagesfromlif01babbgoog/passagesfromlif01babbgoog_djvu.txt}}</ref>

During Lax's time at Cambridge: "the mathematicians were in the saddle, and it would be difficult to dispute the judgement that they controlled Cambridge studies almost as completely as the [[logician]]s had done in the [[Middle Ages]]."<ref name=autogenerated1>{{cite web |url=https://www.british-history.ac.uk/report.aspx?compid=66632 |title=The University of Cambridge - The age of Newton and Bentley (1660-1800) |author=J. P. C. Roach |date=1959 |access-date=5 July 2012}}</ref> In early nineteenth century Cambridge "the discipline of mathematics was at the very heart".<ref name="Garland1980">{{cite book|author=Martha McMackin Garland|title=Cambridge Before Darwin: The Ideal of a Liberal Education, 1800-1860|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jdA8AAAAIAAJ|access-date=2 July 2012|date=13 November 1980|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-23319-4|page=28}}</ref> [[Method of Fluxions|Newtonian mathematics]] teaching as exemplified by "Cambridge traditionalists" such as Lax and his generation began to wane as the [[Georgian era]] drew to a close.<ref name=autogenerated6 /> In 1817 [[George Peacock (mathematician)|George Peacock]] successfully introduced the new French mathematics (such as [[Pierre-Simon Laplace]] and [[Joseph Louis Lagrange]]) into the [[Cambridge Mathematical Tripos|Senate House Examinations]]. Peacock reported to Herschel, "The introduction of [[Differentiation under the integral sign|d's]] into the papers excited much remark. [[James Wood (mathematician)|Wood]], [[Samuel Vince|Vince]], Lax & [[Isaac Milner|Milner]] were very angry & threatened to protest against [the infiltration of] French mathematics."<ref name="KnoxNoakes2003">{{cite book|author1=Kevin C. Knox|author2=Richard Noakes|title=From Newton to Hawking: A History of Cambridge University's Lucasian Professors of Mathematics|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QGX_rAeia4kC|access-date=6 July 2012|date=6 November 2003|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-66310-6|page=235}}</ref> For the traditionalists the struggle was more than one of intellectual difference as for them, "Newton's rational mechanics, fluxions, and experimental philosophy were an excellent antidote against materialism and atheism."<ref>Kevin C. Knox, 'Milner, Isaac (1750–1820)’, Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, Oxford University Press, 2004 [http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/18788, accessed 24 December 2011]</ref> However, from 1816 to 1824 Lax continued to sit on the Peacock-led board that established [[Cambridge Observatory]].<ref name="Annals of the Solar Physics Observatory, Cambridge Vol. 1">{{cite book|title=Annals of the Solar Physics Observatory, Cambridge|volume= 1|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YBM9AAAAIAAJ&pg=PA16|access-date=6 July 2012|publisher=CUP Archive|page=3|id=GGKEY:RA1CLPY8NJY}}</ref>

Lax did encounter some criticism during his tenure. Whilst at the university he "never, as far as is known, delivered a single lecture", despite his chair's [[bequest]] that the holder deliver forty lectures each year, although his predecessor had not given any lectures either.<ref name="Garrett2004">{{cite book|author=Martin Garrett|title=Cambridge: A Cultural and Literary History|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2-gCqtMfi-YC|access-date=2 July 2012|date=2004|publisher=Signal Books|isbn=978-1-902669-79-3|page=70}}</ref><ref name="Ball1889">{{cite book|author=Walter William Rouse Ball|title=A history of the study of mathematics at Cambridge|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AFcPAQAAMAAJ|access-date=9 July 2012|date=1889|publisher=University Press|page=105}}</ref> The excuse was made that there was already an astronomical chair at Cambridge established before the Lowndean that already gave lectures.<ref name=autogenerated7 /> By the 1820s it was no longer acceptable to consider chairs as sinecures, and Lax received criticism from a living descendant of the original benefactor, [[Thomas Lowndes (astronomer)|Thomas Lowndes]], for being remiss in his duties.<ref name=autogenerated7 /> His successor to the Lowndean chair George Peacock promised "to do his duty in a less lax manner than his predecessor", and although he struggled to get anyone to attend his lectures on pure mathematics, his lectures on practical astronomy were well attended.<ref name=autogenerated6>Harvey W. Becher, 'Peacock, George (1791–1858)’, Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, Oxford University Press, 2004; online edn, May 2009 [http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/21673, accessed 25 December 2011]</ref> However, Peacock's translation as [[Dean of Ely]] three years later meant that he was largely absent from his chair, which he was severely criticised for retaining.<ref name="Craik2008">{{cite book|author=Alex D. D. Craik|title=Mr Hopkins' Men: Cambridge Reform and British Mathematics in the 19th Century|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=te4t81kg1JQC|access-date=2 July 2012|date=19 February 2008|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-1-84800-132-9|page=66}}</ref><ref name="Cannell2001">{{cite book|author=Doris Mary Cannell|title=George Green: Mathematician & Physicist, 1793-1841 : the Background to His Life and Work|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=x2Y2eb9IzwwC|access-date=2 July 2012|date=2001|publisher=SIAM|isbn=978-0-89871-463-0|page=91}}</ref>

===Fellow of the Royal Society===
[[File:SomersetHousebyAnonpublAckermann&Co1836.jpg|thumb|upright|left|[[Somerset House]] in 1836, where the Royal Society met in Lax's time.]]
Lax was admitted a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] on 5 April 1796. He was nominated by the [[Astronomer Royal]] [[Nevil Maskelyne]], [[Anthony Shepherd]], [[Richard Farmer]] and [[William Wales (astronomer)|William Wales]].<ref>{{cite web|title=William Lax EC/1796/05 GB 117|url=http://www2.royalsociety.org/DServe/dserve.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqCmd=Show.tcl&dsqSearch=RefNo==%27EC%2F1796%2F05%27&dsqDb=Catalog|publisher=The Royal Society|access-date=14 July 2012}}</ref> However, due to an enmity of the President [[Joseph Banks]], friends of [[Charles Hutton]] and Maskelyne, such as Lax, [[Samuel Vince]] and [[Thomas Mudge (horologist)|Thomas Mudge]], frequently saw their submissions for publications overlooked.<ref name="Gascoigne2003">{{cite book|author=John Gascoigne|title=Joseph Banks and the English Enlightenment: Useful Knowledge and Polite Culture|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lkJ6Y7XRy9QC|access-date=2 July 2012|date=18 December 2003|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-54211-1|page=254}}</ref> If any of them submitted papers to the [[Royal Society|Society]]: <blockquote>they had the honour of having them carefully lodged in the archives of the Society, where the world in general, or even the members of the Society, would derive no more benefit from them than if they were deposited at the centre of the earth.<ref name="WebsterTreadwell1826">{{cite book|author1=John White Webster|author2=Daniel Treadwell|author3=John Ware|title=The Boston journal of philosophy and the arts|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=n94RAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA288|access-date=2 July 2012|date=1826|publisher=Cummings, Hilliard, & Co.|page=416}}</ref></blockquote>

Lax delivered two papers to the Royal Society which were published in ''[[Philosophical Transactions]]''. In 1799 he delivered ''A Method of finding the Latitude of a place, by Means of two Altitudes of the Sun and the Time elapsed betwixt the Observations''. It was described as "a very valuable paper" by [[Abraham Rees]], and apparently contained "several valuable remarks", but it was criticised as "a subject of no great importance" by the ''[[Philosophical Magazine]]''.<ref name="Rees1819">{{cite book|author=Abraham Rees|title=The Cyclopædia, Or, Universal Dictionary of Arts, Sciences, and Literature|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rvH8ra5JriwC&pg=PP353|year=1819|publisher=Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme & Brown|page=353}}</ref><ref name="Overall1870">{{cite book|author=William Henry Overall |author-link=William Henry Overall|title=The dictionary of chronology, or historical and statistical register|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pwluAAAAMAAJ|access-date=2 July 2012|date=1870|publisher=W. Tegg|page=479}}</ref><ref name=autogenerated12>{{cite journal |date=1837 |journal=London and Edinburgh Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science |volume=LX |page=150 |title=The Royal Society. Address of His Royal Highness the President (pp. 141–154)|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-EwwAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA150 }}</ref> In his 1809 work ''On A Method of Examining the Divisions of Astronomical Instruments'' Lax wrote that no instrument was to be trusted without "previous examination".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lax |first1=William |date=1809 |title=On A Method of Examining the Divisions of Astronomical Instruments |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society |volume=99 |pages=232–245 |publisher=The Royal Society |doi= 10.1098/rstl.1809.0016|jstor=107263 |bibcode = 1809RSPT...99..232L |s2cid=110947378 }}</ref> This argument had an influence on scientists such as [[Henry Cavendish]] and was described as an "ingenious...examination" in the ''[[Edinburgh Encyclopedia]]''.<ref>{{cite book |title=Cavendish: The Experimental Life |last1=Jungnickel |first1=Christa|author1-link= Christa Jungnickel|last2=McCormmach|first2=Russell|year=1999 |author2-link=Russell McCormmach |publisher=Bucknell University Press |isbn=978-0838754450 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/cavendishexperim00jung }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=The Edinburgh Encyclopædia |last=Brewster |first=David |page=834 }}</ref> However the method described by Lax "though very ingenious, requires great labour and time, and is inferior in accuracy and efficiency to that which was adopted by [[Edward Troughton|Mr. Troughton]] for tabulating the errors of the primary divisions of circular instruments."<ref name=autogenerated12 /> It was also criticised for "greatly resembl[ing]" a method first explicated by the [[Duke of Chaulnes]].<ref name="Tomlinson1852">{{cite book|author=Charles Tomlinson|title=Cyclopædia of useful arts, mechanical and chemical, manufactures, mining, and engineering|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HzFRAAAAYAAJ|access-date=2 July 2012|date=1852|publisher=G. Virtue|page=795}}</ref> In 1807 Lax delivered ''Remarks on a Supposed Error in the Elements of Euclid'' to the Royal Society, however it was not published in ''Philosophical Transactions'', but was eventually published independently. In it Lax defended the Greek mathematician against a charge levied at him by [[Georges-Louis Le Sage]] in 1756. Lax's defence was applauded by the ''[[British Critic]]'' as 'perfectly sound'.<ref name="The British critic">{{cite book|title=The British critic|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BbDQAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA303|access-date=21 July 2012|date=1809|publisher=Printed for F. and C. Rivington|page=303}}</ref> Lax also espoused the worth of [[Euclid's Elements|Euclid's ''Elements'']] in the work, which he considered to reflect "the highest honour upon the human intellect".<ref name="Lax1807">{{cite book|author=William Lax|title=Remarks on a supposed error in the Elements of Euclid|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DOlbAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA14|publisher=Cambridge University Press|access-date=2 July 2012|date=1807|page=3}}</ref>

===Board of Longitude===
Lax was elected to the [[Board of Longitude]] after he was nominated to the Lowndean chair in 1795, and remained on the board until it was dissolved in 1828.<ref name="The Nautical Almanac and Astronomical Ephemeris for the Year ...">{{cite book|title=The Nautical Almanac and Astronomical Ephemeris for the Year ...|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fAgAAAAAMAAJ&pg=PP13|access-date=22 April 2013|date=1800|publisher=order of the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty|page=13}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Thomas Young: Natural Philosopher 1773-1829 |last=Wood |first=Alexander |date=2011 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0521263764 |page=343 }}</ref> The Board was a governmental body charged with administering a scheme of prizes intended to encourage innovators to solve the problem of finding [[longitude]] at sea, which was vital for accurate navigation. Lax published a set of tables for use with the ''Nautical Almanac'' for finding [[latitude]] and longitude; these were published by the Board of Longitude in 1821, and whilst they were not considered to be of much practical use for seamen, they were described by ''[[The Nautical Magazine]]'' as a "very meritorious attempt to solve the problems of nautical astronomy by one uniform system."<ref name="The Nautical magazine: a journal of papers on subjects connected with maritime affairs">{{cite book|title=The Nautical magazine: a journal of papers on subjects connected with maritime affairs|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6YwEAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA281|access-date=2 July 2012|date=1832|publisher=Brown, Son and Ferguson|page=256}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |journal=The Nautical Magazine |year=1840 |volume=9 |page=897 |title=in pages 896–899 of Review of ''The Practice of Navigational and Nautical Astronomy'' by H. Raper |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=nyp.33433066364781;view=1up;seq=917}}</ref> In 1821, the Board awarded Lax £1050 for his tables, which were intended to replace [[Nevil Maskelyne]]'s ''Requisite Tables''.<ref>[http://cudl.lib.cam.ac.uk/view/MS-RGO-00014-00007/531 Papers of the Board of Longitude : Confirmed minutes of the Board of Longitude, 1802-1823 : 2:369<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> However, the extraordinarily accurate chronometers of [[John Harrison]] were generally available from the 1820s onwards, rendering the [[lunar distance method]], which Lax had used to create the tables, immaterial. Meanwhile, [[Edward Sabine]] criticised errors in Lax's work.<ref name="Sabine1825">{{cite book|author=Edward Sabine |author-link=Edward Sabine|title=An account of experiments to determine the figure of the earth: by means of the pendulum vibrating seconds in different latitudes, as well as on various other subjects of philosophical inquiry|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9ow_AAAAcAAJ|access-date=2 July 2012|date=1825|publisher=J. Murray|page=398}}</ref>

As a scientific member of the Board, Lax was one of eighteen men who were, according to Edmund Dews, "ultimately responsible for the form and contents of the ''Nautical Almanac''. It would have been difficult in these years to select another group equally eminent in their field."<ref name=autogenerated14>{{cite book |title=Thomas Young: Natural Philosopher 1773-1829 |last=Wood |first=Alexander |date=2011 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0521263764 |page=344 }}</ref> Lax was notable for his strong attendance record at the quarterly meetings, not missing a single meeting between 1822 – 25, a record equalled by only three other members, although non-attendance of meetings would have resulted in his not being paid his annual salary of £100.<ref name=autogenerated14 /> In 1828 Lax appended ''An easy method of correcting the lunar distance, on account of the spheroidal figure of the earth'' to the ''Nautical Almanac''. After the Board was dissolved in 1828 Lax unsuccessfully attempted to convince George Biddell Airy to aid in a campaign for its restoration.<ref name=autogenerated8>{{cite book|author1=George Biddell Airy|author2=Wilfred Airy|title=Autobiography of Sir George Biddell Airy|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=f1zaHfblHvUC|access-date=2 July 2012|date=24 June 2010|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-108-00894-5|page=85}}</ref> In 1834 a new edition of his nautical tables was published posthumously.<ref name=autogenerated9 /> [[Eva Germaine Rimington Taylor]] later concluded that all of Lax's works were "of value to the art of navigation".<ref name="TaylorNavigation1966">{{cite book|author1=Eva Germaine Rimington Taylor|author2=Institute of Navigation|title=The mathematical practitioners of Hanoverian England, 1714-1840|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NgE6AAAAMAAJ|access-date=2 July 2012|date=1966|publisher=Cambridge U.P. for the Institute of Navigation|page=316}}</ref>

==Personal life==
[[File:St. Ippolyts Church, Herts - geograph.org.uk - 118233.jpg|thumb|upright|right|St Ippolyts Church]]
On 28 February 1801 Lax was granted the livings as vicar of [[Marsworth]], [[Buckinghamshire]] and [[wikt:squarson|squarson]] of [[Great Wymondley]] with [[St Ippolyts]] near [[Hitchin]], [[Hertfordshire]] "after some years of teaching work".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://cs-test.ias.ac.in/cs/Downloads/article_1393.pdf |title=Lax, William (1761 – 1836) |access-date=2 July 2012 |archive-date=19 April 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120419002103/http://cs-test.ias.ac.in/cs/Downloads/article_1393.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> He lived at St Ippolyts where he erected a private [[observatory]] which he had transported from Cambridge and had originally belonged to [[Isaac Newton]].<ref name=autogenerated9 /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Anderson |first1=S. J. |date=1981 |title=The Reverend William Lax and a Supposed Observatory of Newton's (Letter to the editor) |journal=Journal of the British Astronomical Association |volume=92 |issue=December |page=42 |url=https://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/full/1981JBAA...92...42A |bibcode=1981JBAA...92...42A}}</ref> [[Charles Hutton]]'s 1815 list of England's 20 most notable private observatories (excluding the King's private observatory) included Professor Lax's.<ref>{{cite book|author=Hutton, Charles|title=A Philosophical and Mathematical Dictionary|year=1815|volume=2|chapter=English observatories (private)|page=129|publisher=Printed for the author etc. |chapter-url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=mdp.39015080121448;view=1up;seq=135}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Evans, L.|authorlink=Lewis Evans (mathematician)|journal=The Monthly Magazine|title=letter of Mr. Evans on the Woolwich Observatory|date=1 July 1816|volume=41|issue=285|pages=483–484|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vzo5AQAAMAAJ&pg=PA483}} Evans pointed out 2 mistakes in Hutton's statements concerning private observatories.</ref><!-- The ''[[Monthly Magazine]]'' included it in its list of the 21 most notable private observatories in England in 1813.<ref>{{cite journal |date=1813 |journal=The Monthly Magazine |issue=2 |page=102 }}</ref> COMMENTED OUT BECAUSE UNABLE TO VERIFY REFERENCE --> Lax spent the last thirty years of his life occupied with "studies and pursuits connected with the advancement of astronomy."<ref name="Britain)1837">{{cite book|author=Royal Society (Great Britain)|title=Proceedings of the Royal Society|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JO8yAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA438|access-date=21 July 2012|date=1837|publisher=The Society|page=438}}</ref>

When he arrived at St Ippolyts Lax had trees planted in the vicarage grounds in the form of his initials "W L".<ref name=autogenerated3>{{cite book |title=The Hertfordshire Village Book |author=Hertfordshire Federation of Women's Institutes |publisher=Countryside Books}}</ref> That same year he created a park opposite to the vicarage similar to [[The Backs]] of Cambridge, built a replica of [[List of bridges in Cambridge#Trinity College Bridge (1764)|Trinity College Bridge]], [[dam]]med the stream and opened [[spring (hydrosphere)|springs]] to form a lake which was used for [[ice skating]] in the winter.<ref name=autogenerated3 /> In September 1801 he married Margaret Cradock (11 June 1776 – 20 January 1854) at the church in [[Gilling West]] in the North Riding of Yorkshire. Margaret was the eldest daughter of Sheldon Cradock of [[Hartforth]] who was the [[lord of the manor]] of Lax's home village of Ravensworth.<ref>{{cite book |title=Dugdale's Visitation of Yorkshire, with additions|volume =3 |last=Dugdale |first=William |access-date=5 July 2012 |url=http://www.ebooksread.com/authors-eng/william-dugdale/dugdales-visitation-of-yorkshire-with-additions-volume-3-dgu/page-25-dugdales-visitation-of-yorkshire-with-additions-volume-3-dgu.shtml}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Marriages |journal=The European Magazine, and London Review |date=September 1801 |volume=40 |page=238 |publisher=Philological Society |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=inu.30000093209322;view=1up;seq=258}}</ref><ref name="GroupBooks2010">{{cite book|author1=Books Group|author2=General Books|title=The Gentleman's Magazine |volume =71|number= 2|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aUjmbwAACAAJ|access-date=2 July 2012|date=March 2010|publisher=General Books LLC|isbn=978-1-154-26102-8|page=859}}</ref> Lax was a proposer of [[Robert Woodhouse]], [[Henry Coddington]], [[Herbert Marsh]] and [[John Bell (barrister)|John Bell]] for Royal Society fellowship, the latter being one of Lax's closest friends, and he was a keen supporter of George Biddell Airy throughout Airy's career.<ref name=autogenerated10 /><ref>{{cite web|title=Woodhouse, Robert EC/1802/08|url=http://royalsociety.org/dserve/dserve.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqDb=Catalog&dsqSearch=RefNo=='EC%2F1802%2F08'&dsqCmd=Show.tcl|work=GB 117|publisher=The Royal Society|access-date=14 July 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Coddington, Henry EC/1829/07|url=http://royalsociety.org/dserve/dserve.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqDb=Catalog&dsqCmd=show.tcl&dsqSearch=(RefNo==%22EC%2F1829%2F07%22)|work=GB 117|publisher=The Royal Society|access-date=14 July 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Marsh, Herbert, Bishop of Peterborough EC/1800/13|url=http://royalsociety.org/dserve/dserve.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqDb=Catalog&dsqSearch=RefNo==%27EC%2F1800%2F13%27&dsqCmd=Show.tcl)|work=GB 117|publisher=The Royal Society|access-date=15 July 2012}}</ref><ref name=autogenerated11>{{cite book|author1=George Biddell Airy|author2=Wilfred Airy|title=Autobiography of Sir George Biddell Airy|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=f1zaHfblHvUC|access-date=2 July 2012|date=24 June 2010|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-108-00894-5}}</ref> Lax was a chief supporter of the [[Whig (British political party)|Whig]] [[John Romilly, 1st Baron Romilly]]'s parliamentary bid.<ref name="Romilly's Cambridge Diary 1832-42">{{cite book|title=Romilly's Cambridge Diary 1832-42|year = 1967|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAI4AAAAIAAJ&pg=PA109|access-date=2 July 2012|publisher=CUP Archive|page=9|id=GGKEY:UL0P398HGG3}}</ref> In 1824 Lax purchased a [[coat of arms]] for himself.<ref name="Berry1828">{{cite book|last=Berry|first=William|title=Encyclopaedia heraldica or complete dictionary of heraldry|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=e_lBAAAAcAAJ&pg=PT537|access-date=26 July 2012|date=1828|publisher=Sherwood, Gilbert and Piper|page=537}}</ref>

His brother Thomas Lax (1770 – 1 Apr 1851) lived in Ravensworth. He was a [[Landed gentry|gentleman]] farmer who became a record holding breeder of [[shorthorn cattle]] and at one point was credited with the best shorthorn herd in the country. He was "unquestionably a great breeder".<ref>{{cite book |title=History of Shorthorn cattle |last=Sinclair |first=James |date=1907 |page=208 |access-date=2 July 2012 |url=https://www.scribd.com/doc/3024592/History-of-Shorthorn-cattle}}</ref> He also acted as [[Chief Constable]] of the [[wapentake]] of [[Gilling West]]. The Kirkby Ravensworth parish church has a memorial dedicated to Thomas Lax, as well as a memorial dedicated to the mother of the two brothers.

==Death==
On 1 December 1834, Lax reported that he had been "of late in a very weak state of health".<ref>Tables to be used with the Nautical almanac for finding the latitude and longitude at sea, 1834. by Lax, William</ref> He died "suddenly" on 29 October 1836 at his home in St Ippolyts.<ref>{{cite news |title=Obituary |newspaper=The Champion |date=6 November 1836 |publisher=Richard Cobbett |location=London|issue=8}}</ref> His obituary in ''[[The Gentleman's Magazine]]'' reported that "his constitution was broken in early life [which] made his last years a period of weakness and suffering, so that his physical strength was unequal to the workings of his active mind. To whatever Professor Lax applied, he made himself completely master of it...[a] most excellent and amiable man."<ref name="The Gentleman's magazine">{{cite book|title=The Gentleman's magazine|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qaklrCCQQgsC&pg=PA656|access-date=21 July 2012|date=1837|publisher=F. Jefferies|page=656}}</ref> He left behind a widow and two daughters, the eldest Margaret and the younger Marian or Marianne (died 21 June 1873).<ref>{{cite journal |journal=The Spectator |year=1839 |volume=12 |page=329 |title=Marriages |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=mdp.39015033541270;view=1up;seq=313}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=Cambridge |newspaper=The Bury and Norwich Post, and Suffolk Herald |date=1 July 1873 |page=7 |issue=4749 }}</ref> In 1826 Margaret was married to [[Andrew Amos (lawyer)|Andrew Amos]] at St Ippolyts Church, and via that line Lax is the grandfather of [[Sheldon Amos]] and the great grandfather of [[Maurice Amos]].<ref>Thomas S. Legg, 'Amos, Andrew (1791–1860)’, Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, Oxford University Press, 2004; online edn, January 2008 [http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/453, accessed 27 November 2011]</ref>
